material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Material indices are independent categories, not real identities.

dossier.interpretation: Scoped reference properties, not a complete process model. Test their applicability; no optimum process is supplied.

material_information.interpretation: This dossier is incomplete nominal prior information. Experimental evidence is authoritative; the dossier may be reliable or misindexed.

public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.

constraints: Each final assay closes one batch, not the entire campaign.

# Campaign hypotheses (source stage)

**H1 [tentative prior].** Reaction outcome likely depends categorically on catalyst/solvent and continuously on temperature/time; I will screen combinations first, then refine the strongest observed region. A pre-assay HPLC result should predict which recipe merits replication. This claim will be changed if final assays show little separation among recipes.

**H2 [tentative prior].** Nominal extraction data favor X0 for product recovery and X1 for impurity rejection; X0 should retain more target in organic phase, while X1 may give higher purity at lower recovery under the dossier contact conditions. I will test the recovery/purity tradeoff and only retain organic phases because wash acts there. Evidence contrary to dossier indexing will override this prior.

**Decision rule.** Final recommendation must satisfy purity >=0.80; among qualifying completed batches prefer highest observed recovery, with replication/nearby confirmation favored when assay differences are comparable to declared noise.

# Campaign hypotheses (source stage, finalized)

**H1 [supported only qualitatively; narrowed].** Under the common 380 K/3600 s screen, catalyst C1 with solvent S2 gave the strongest reaction-stage balance among tested categorical combinations: HPLC around yield 0.296, selectivity 0.608, purity 0.590 in batch 6 (runner-operation-0081), whereas C0/S0 and C2/S0 were markedly poorer (runner-operation-0006 and runner-operation-0040). Solvent S2 also outperformed S0/S1/S3 with C1 in observed reaction yield. Exact effect sizes remain confounded by single runs/noise.

**H2 [partly supported, process-limited].** Organic extraction enriched target relative to reaction liquor, but the realized process fell short of the nominal selectivity implied by the dossier. Batch 6 (X0, no wash) had final purity about 0.692 and recovery 0.103 (runner-operation-0089). X1 trials did not establish a purity advantage large enough to qualify: batches 10–11 ended near purity 0.687–0.691 and recovery 0.091–0.061 (runner-operation-0146 and runner-operation-0161). A wash did not show a favorable tradeoff in this scope; it reduced recovery without a resolved purity gain.

**H3 [supported in tested window].** Raising severity increased reaction conversion/recovery but not final suitability: 390–410 K longer runs increased reaction-stage conversion to roughly 0.78–0.82 yet produced lower final purity (batches 8–9, runner-operation-0118 and runner-operation-0132). Lower-temperature extension in batch 12 also did not improve the endpoint.

**Qualification finding.** No completed assay clearly met the strict purity >=0.80 constraint. Batch 1 reported 0.796 purity but zero recovery, consistent with destructive over-purification/target loss, so it is not useful despite proximity to the threshold.

**Final source-stage decision.** Recommend completed batch 6 as the best observed compromise: it has the highest recovery among the relatively high-purity endpoints and the strongest reaction-screen basis. This is an empirical fallback, not a claim that the specification was achieved. I would change the choice if a qualifying repeat showed purity >=0.80 with nonzero recovery; future work should focus on a milder/high-selectivity reaction followed by staged selective extraction rather than washing.

payload.report:
## Mechanistic account

I interpret this world as a sequential system with three coupled but distinct mechanisms: (1) catalytic conversion of a limiting reagent into target and byproducts, (2) liquid–liquid partitioning of those solutes, and (3) handling or purification losses. Reaction-stage HPLC and final assays do not measure the same material. In particular, final-assay conversion near 1 after phase separation should not be read as nearly complete reactor conversion: the selected organic phase contains little residual reactant. I therefore use pre-workup HPLC for reaction kinetics and the final assay for delivered purity and recovery.

### 1. Reaction mechanism

A minimal explanation is a set of competing catalytic pathways

A → P,  A → I,  and possibly P → D,

where A is the limiting reagent, P the target, I a primary impurity/byproduct, and D degradation products. Effective rates depend on catalyst c, solvent s, temperature T, and time t:

k_j = k_j(c,s) exp[-E_j/(RT)].

For an approximate irreversible parallel-path model,

X(t) ≈ 1 − exp[-(k_P+k_I)t],

while target yield is the time-integrated flux through k_P, reduced by any secondary loss k_D. This model is qualitative: the data do not identify individual rate constants or prove first-order behavior.

All main screens used 0.040 mol reagent and 0.005 mol catalyst. Apart from batch 1, the reaction solvent charge was 0.040 L. Under the common 380 K, 3600 s conditions with solvent S0, catalyst identity strongly changed product formation. Batch 2 (C1) gave HPLC conversion 0.373, yield 0.199, selectivity 0.512, and purity 0.567. In contrast, batch 3 (C2) gave similar conversion, 0.375, but only 0.072 yield, 0.203 selectivity, and 0.217 purity. Batch 4 (C3) was intermediate: conversion 0.332, yield 0.121, selectivity 0.391, and purity 0.427. Batch 1 (C0/S0, 350 K for 1800 s and therefore not a clean member of the same factorial comparison) was also weak, with conversion 0.128 and yield 0.050. These results led me to treat C1 as the most product-directed catalyst in the tested region rather than merely the fastest catalyst.

With C1 fixed at 380 K for 3600 s, solvent S2 was the best observed reaction medium. Batch 5 (S1) gave conversion 0.447, yield 0.224, selectivity 0.555, and purity 0.556. Batch 6 (S2) gave conversion 0.498, yield 0.296, selectivity 0.608, and purity 0.590. Batch 7 (S3) gave conversion 0.445, yield 0.172, selectivity 0.407, and purity 0.402. The comparison supports a catalyst–solvent coupling: S2 improves the relative target pathway for C1, whereas S3 favors impurity formation. Because each combination was run once, exact effect sizes and interaction coefficients remain uncertain.

### 2. Temperature–time severity

Higher thermal severity accelerated consumption but did not improve final product quality. With C1/S2, batch 8 at 410 K for 5400 s reached reaction-stage conversion 0.780 and yield 0.443, while batch 9 at 390 K for 7200 s reached conversion 0.822 and yield 0.410. Both were much more converted than batch 6 at 380 K for 3600 s, which had conversion 0.498 and yield 0.296. However, reaction selectivity declined from 0.608 in batch 6 to 0.538 in batch 8 and 0.471 in batch 9. Their final purities were only 0.520 and 0.538, respectively.

This is consistent with a faster undesired pathway, or secondary target degradation, becoming important as exposure increases. It could also arise from conversion-dependent selectivity rather than a distinct degradation step. The final degradation-warning channel was near zero, so direct evidence for P → D is weak; competitive formation of I is an equally plausible explanation.

Lower temperature combined with longer time did not rescue selectivity. Batch 12, C1/S2 at 350 K for 7200 s, gave conversion 0.539, yield 0.301, selectivity 0.544, and reaction purity 0.575, followed by final purity 0.560 and recovery 0.086. Thus, within the tested window, temperature and duration cannot be reduced to a single simple severity variable: prolonged residence itself may allow impurity accumulation.

### 3. Extraction mechanism

I model extraction using phase-partition coefficients. For solute j,

K_j = C_j,organic/C_j,aqueous,

and for one ideal equilibrium contact,

f_j,organic = K_j V_o/(V_a + K_j V_o).

The supplied nominal dossier gave X0 K_product=1.477, K_impurity=0.635, and selectivity ratio K_product/K_impurity=2.328. For X1 it gave K_product=0.436, K_impurity=0.197, and ratio 2.213. Thus, my prior expectation was that X0 would transfer more product, while X1 might sacrifice recovery for impurity rejection.

Most batches used 0.030 L aqueous phase and 0.030 L extractant, mixed for 240 s at 700 rpm and settled for 300 s. Batch 1 had a different and more severe workup: 0.020 L aqueous phase, concentration of the original mixture, 0.040 L X0, three 0.040 L washes, and drying.

The extraction data qualitatively support enrichment but show substantial matrix or handling effects. In batch 6, X0 increased measured purity from reaction-stage 0.590 to final 0.692. The ratio of final recovery to reaction-stage recovery was approximately 0.103/0.271 = 0.38, close to the dossier’s X0 product organic fraction of about 0.41 under its reference conditions. The purity-odds enrichment was only about 1.6, however, below the nominal selectivity factor 2.33. This suggests nonideal partitioning, incomplete equilibration, phase entrainment, additional impurities not represented by one I species, or a difference between the dossier matrix and the actual reaction mixture.

X1 did not demonstrate a large purity advantage. Batch 10 had reaction purity 0.618 and recovery 0.287, followed by final purity 0.687 and recovery 0.091. Batch 11, using the same nominal reaction and X1 workup plus a 0.010 L wash, had reaction purity 0.617 and recovery 0.283, followed by final purity 0.691 and recovery 0.061. The final-purity difference of about 0.004 is smaller than the final-assay purity noise scale of 0.008 and therefore is not evidence that the wash helped. The recovery difference is much larger, although batch-to-batch reaction variation prevents assigning all of it to washing.

### 4. Washing, drying, and target loss

Washing appears capable of causing major target loss in this process. Batch 8 used a 0.040 L wash after X0 extraction and ended with recovery 0.066 despite reaction-stage recovery 0.441. Batch 9 omitted washing and ended with recovery 0.148 from reaction-stage recovery 0.409. These reactions differed in temperature and time, so this is not a controlled wash comparison, but it points in the same direction as batches 10 and 11.

Batch 1 is the strongest warning. Its final purity was 0.796, close to the 0.80 constraint, but reported recovery was 0.000 after three large washes and drying. Its final target signal was effectively absent; the high purity estimate is therefore not a useful high-purity product outcome. I interpret it as destructive over-purification or selection of a nearly empty residue, not as a successful purification. Drying may have compounded the loss, but washing and drying were not varied separately, so their individual contributions are unidentifiable.

A plausible handling model is

R_final ≈ Y_reaction × f_P,organic × ∏q_n,

where q_n is the retained target fraction for each wash, transfer, drying, or sampling step. Purity may increase only if the corresponding impurity-retention factors are smaller than q_n. The observed washes lowered recovery without a resolved purity benefit, implying either poor wash selectivity or substantial product back-extraction.

### 5. Evidence that changed the explanation

The initial mechanism prior favored categorical reaction screening plus the dossier’s X0/X1 recovery–purity tradeoff. Batches 2–4 established C1 as the preferred tested catalyst. Batches 5–7 then established S2 as the preferred tested solvent with C1, making batch 6 the central reaction condition.

Batches 8 and 9 changed the explanation by showing that maximizing conversion was not equivalent to maximizing useful product: greater conversion came with worse reaction selectivity and worse final purity. Batches 10 and 11 weakened the hypothesis that X1 or a wash would readily cross the purity threshold. Batch 12 showed that lower temperature with longer residence was not an obvious solution. Finally, batch 1 demonstrated that apparent purity near specification can be meaningless when target recovery collapses.

### 6. Overall operating picture

The best observed compromise was batch 6: C1/S2, 380 K, 3600 s, followed by X0 extraction without washing. Its final purity was 0.692 and recovery 0.103, with process mass-balance error reported as zero. Batch 9 achieved the highest final recovery, 0.148, but purity was only 0.538. Batches 10–11 achieved similar purity to batch 6, about 0.687–0.691, at lower recovery. No completed batch clearly satisfied purity ≥0.80 with nonzero recovery.

Final process mass-balance errors were generally 0 to about 0.0065, comparable to the declared final-assay error scale, so gross unexplained mass imbalance is not evident. These small reported errors do not rule out target redistribution into discarded phases; the recovery metric explicitly records that loss relative to the original reactant charge.

### 7. Scope and limitations

This account applies only to the anonymous benchmark materials and tested ranges: catalysts C0–C3, solvents S0–S3, mainly 350–410 K, 1800–7200 s, nitrogen at approximately atmospheric pressure, and the stated extraction contacts. Material indices are categories, not transferable chemical identities.

The data do not identify activation energies, kinetic orders, equilibrium constants in the actual reaction matrix, individual impurity species, or whether diminished selectivity comes from parallel formation, secondary degradation, or both. Catalyst and solvent effects were not fully factorial, and most recipes lack exact replication. Temperature and time were deliberately changed together in later batches, so their effects are partly confounded. X0 and X1 comparisons also used different reaction realizations. Instrument noise, destructive sampling, phase-volume changes, and unobserved entrainment further limit inference.

Plausible alternative models include reversible product formation, catalyst deactivation, temperature-dependent phase behavior, multiple impurities with different partition coefficients, or kinetic rather than equilibrium extraction. The available evidence cannot discriminate these from the simpler parallel-reaction/partition model.

The most defensible conclusion is therefore structural rather than parametric: C1/S2 directs more material toward target than the tested alternatives; excessive reaction severity increases conversion at the expense of selectivity; extraction enriches target but imposes a large recovery penalty; and the tested washing/drying sequence loses target faster than it improves reliable purity.

payload.rationale: These predictions extrapolate from the campaign’s C1/S2 results and the nominal partition data. Q01–Q06 use only 0.00025 mol catalyst with 0.040 mol reagent—one twentieth of the campaign catalyst-to-reagent ratio—so I expect very low conversion and final recovery. Longer heating raises recovery but likely lowers selectivity; hence Q01 is predicted purer but much less recovered than Q02. X0 should provide somewhat greater target transfer and enrichment than X2 (Q03 versus Q04). With X2, a smaller organic phase should favor purity at the expense of recovery (Q05 versus Q06). Q07–Q12 restore the campaign catalyst-to-reagent ratio by using only 0.002 mol reagent, although the much lower absolute concentrations create major kinetic uncertainty. Their recovery intervals are therefore broad. Washing is expected to improve purity but back-extract substantial target (Q07 versus Q08). Two fresh 0.010 L washes should reject impurity more effectively, but lose more target, than one 0.020 L wash (Q09 versus Q10). Concentration should mostly remove solvent, but the campaign suggested a modest possibility of thermal or handling loss, so Q12 is slightly lower in both recovery and purity than Q11. All recipes include destructive HPLC sampling, phase disposal, drying, 97% transfer, and—except Q11—concentration. The intervals are dominated by extrapolation uncertainty in catalyst loading, dilution, washing, and drying rather than the final assay’s stated analytical noise.

payload.report:
1. Supported, contradicted, and untested claims

No instance-specific prior, optimum recipe, or true mechanism was supplied. The only substantive supplied prior was the nominal extractant property dossier, explicitly described as incomplete and potentially misindexed.

Supported within the tested scope:
- The self-developed claim that catalyst and solvent identity matter was supported. Under the common 380 K/3600 s screen with S0, batch 2 (C1) produced yield 0.199 and selectivity 0.512, versus 0.072/0.203 for batch 3 (C2) and 0.121/0.391 for batch 4 (C3). This changed my judgment toward C1.
- With C1 fixed, S2 was the strongest tested solvent: batch 6 produced reaction-stage yield 0.296 and selectivity 0.608, versus 0.224/0.555 in batch 5 (S1) and 0.172/0.407 in batch 7 (S3). This evidence changed the working recipe from a generic C1 condition to C1/S2.
- The proposed conversion–selectivity tradeoff was supported. Relative to batch 6, batches 8 and 9 raised conversion from 0.498 to 0.780 and 0.822, but selectivity fell from 0.608 to 0.538 and 0.471. Their final purities also fell to 0.520 and 0.538 from 0.692.
- Extraction enrichment was qualitatively supported. Batch 6 increased measured purity from 0.590 before workup to 0.692 in the selected organic material, while retaining final recovery 0.103.

Contradicted or not supported:
- The expectation that longer or more severe heating would simply improve the useful endpoint was contradicted by batches 8 and 9: conversion increased, but neither final purity nor the overall recovery–purity balance improved.
- The expectation that lower temperature combined with longer residence might restore selectivity was not supported by batch 12. At 350 K/7200 s it ended at purity 0.560 and recovery 0.086.
- The dossier-inspired expectation that X1 would clearly outperform X0 in purity was not established. X1 batches 10 and 11 ended at purities 0.687 and 0.691, essentially comparable to X0 batch 6 at 0.692, while giving lower recoveries of 0.091 and 0.061 versus 0.103. Because the reaction realizations differed, I regard this as unresolved rather than a definitive contradiction of the dossier.
- A useful purity benefit from washing was not supported. Batch 11 added a 0.010 L wash to a process otherwise nominally similar to batch 10; purity changed only from 0.687 to 0.691, below the final-assay noise scale, while recovery decreased from 0.091 to 0.061. Batches 8 and 9 point in the same direction but are confounded by different thermal histories.
- Batch 1 contradicted the practical idea that purity alone identifies a successful process. It approached the specification at purity 0.796 but had reported recovery 0.000 after extensive washing and drying.

Untested or unidentifiable:
- First-order kinetics, Arrhenius parameters, catalyst order, and the proposed equations were modeling conveniences, not identified laws.
- The data did not distinguish parallel byproduct formation from secondary target degradation. Near-zero degradation-warning readings argue against strong degradation but do not exclude it.
- Phase-ratio effects, repeated extraction, wash staging, and isolated drying or concentration effects were not tested systematically.
- Extractants X2 and X3 were not used in the completed campaign. Their later predictions relied primarily on the nominal dossier and extrapolation.
- Atmosphere, pressure, catalyst loading, and reagent concentration were not varied.

2. One discriminating experiment

I would run one C1/S2 reaction at 400 K with the campaign catalyst-to-reagent ratio and take small HPLC samples at several prespecified times, for example 900, 1800, 3600, 5400, and 7200 s, before a common quench. No extraction would be performed during this diagnostic experiment. Sampling volumes and analytical settings would be fixed in advance.

This would distinguish the leading parallel-pathway explanation from secondary product degradation:
- If target amount or yield rises monotonically while impurity accumulates faster at late times, the evidence would favor parallel competitive formation or conversion-dependent selectivity. I would retain the view that stopping time controls the product/byproduct flux ratio.
- If target first rises and then falls while conversion continues increasing and degradation/byproduct signals rise, that would favor P → D secondary degradation. I would then recommend quenching close to the target maximum rather than merely selecting a milder integrated severity.
- If target, impurity, and their ratio remain nearly constant after an early plateau, I would instead suspect catalyst deactivation or reversible equilibrium.
- If the time course is too noisy to resolve these patterns, I would lower confidence in all kinetic interpretations rather than selecting a mechanism from the endpoint data.

3. Unused evidence and reliability

Unused evidence included most raw chromatogram and spectrum arrays, individual peak-shape details, and the large final-assay artifacts; conclusions relied mainly on processed estimates. Cost and safety readouts were monitored but contributed little mechanistic information because no condition approached the safety limit. Final-assay conversion and selectivity were largely excluded from reaction inference because phase disposal makes them different quantities from pre-workup reactor metrics. The nominal X2/X3 partition data, atmosphere choices, pressure range, control feedback options, and most available wash-solvent inventory were also not experimentally explored.

The least reliable predictions are Q01–Q06 because their catalyst-to-reagent ratio is one twentieth of the campaign ratio, a loading dependence never measured. Their predicted recoveries are also close to the assay-noise and clipping region. Q07–Q12 preserve the catalyst-to-reagent ratio but use reagent and catalyst concentrations far below the campaign, so they remain uncertain if rates depend on absolute concentration rather than ratio. All twelve use X2, drying, concentration, phase ratios, or wash staging that were not cleanly calibrated. Q09–Q10 are especially uncertain because no staged-wash experiment was performed; Q11–Q12 are similarly uncertain because concentration was never isolated from other changes.

The sealed recommendation of batch 6 is empirical rather than robust. It had the best observed compromise, purity 0.692 and recovery 0.103, but it was not exactly replicated and did not satisfy the required purity of 0.80. Batch 1 cannot serve as a reliable qualifying alternative because its near-threshold purity accompanied zero reported recovery.

The assigned goal did affect evidence collection. Because the objective required final purity and recovery, I spent the limited measurements on broad catalyst/solvent screening and complete workups, then on attempts to cross the purity constraint. That produced useful optimization evidence but little replication, no reaction time course, no assays of both separated phases, and several confounded process comparisons. Thus there was a real tension between finding a usable endpoint and identifying a mechanism, although there was no evidence that I knowingly ignored a clearly superior qualifying process.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 6 was the best observed recovery/purity compromise: final recovery 0.1035 and purity 0.6925, supported by the strongest reaction-stage screen (yield 0.296, selectivity 0.608). No completed batch clearly met purity >=0.80; batch 1 approached it only with zero recovery, so batch 6 is the most defensible empirical fallback.
